title: A Quantum-Inspired Two-Dimensional Lattice Polarized Radiative Transfer Simulator
authors: Shan Zeng, Bing Lin, Ali Omar
abstract: A quantum inspired framework was developed for polarized radiative transfer in the atmosphere to jointly model multiple scattering, absorption, and emission processes. The radiative field is represented by the Stokes vector and discretized using an n-directional two-dimensional spatial lattice on 3-dimensional uniformly distributed zenith and azimuth angular vectors. The formulation of this quantum computation system is based on the Lattice Boltzmann Method, which incorporates a physics-based polarized phase matrix. A classical lattice solver employing identical spatial and angular discretization and physical modeling as in quantum algorithm is implemented. The corresponding quantum algorithm is evaluated using the IBM Qiskit quantum simulator, enabling direct comparison of numerical accuracy to a classical simulation reference. The results demonstrate that fully physics-based polarized radiative transfer can be embedded within a quantum lattice framework, which provides an initial benchmark toward scalable quantum atmospheric radiative transfer and future quantum climate modeling
summary: This paper proposes a quantum-inspired framework to simulate polarized radiative transfer in the atmosphere using a lattice Boltzmann approach. By mapping physical processes like scattering and absorption into quantum operators, the authors demonstrate that the quantum circuit accurately reproduces classical simulation results. This establishes a crucial benchmark for future quantum climate and atmospheric modeling.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of simulating polarized radiative transfer in the atmosphere, which requires jointly modeling multiple scattering, absorption, and emission processes.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated that the full physics of polarized radiative transfer can be embedded within a quantum lattice framework, with quantum and classical results agreeing to high precision.
method: They developed a quantum-inspired approach based on the Lattice Boltzmann Method, mapping the physical processes (emission, scattering, absorption) into sequences of quantum operators implemented on a quantum simulator.
model_or_system: The system is the Earth's atmosphere, modeled using the Stokes vector to track polarization. The simulation uses a D2Q9 lattice stencil and is implemented via quantum circuits on the IBM Qiskit simulator.
key_observables: Stokes vector components (I, Q, U, V), Degree of Polarization (DOP), and the absolute/relative differences between quantum and classical solutions.
important_parameters: The simulation uses a D2Q9 stencil, and the resource scaling shows qubit requirements grow significantly with the number of time steps.
main_assumptions: The primary assumptions involve discretizing the continuous physical domain onto a lattice and approximating complex physical interactions (like scattering) using quantum operators.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the D1Q2 and D2Q9 lattice schematics, the quantum radiative transfer coding structure, and show comparisons of intensity, polarization, and DOP time series between quantum and classical solvers.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the physical problem and the quantum-inspired LBM framework. It then details the mapping of physical processes (Emission, Scattering, Absorption) into quantum operators. Finally, it presents extensive comparisons between the quantum and classical solvers across various spatial, temporal, and angular configurations.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, physics-based blueprint for mapping a complex, continuous wave propagation problem (RTE) onto a discrete quantum circuit structure, which is highly relevant for quantum simulation of open quantum systems.
